A regular hexagon with side length 4 is subdivided into a lattice of 96 equilateral triangles of side length 1. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of this lattice. Compute the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in $S$ that contain the center of the hexagon strictly in their interior.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(O\) be the center of the hexagon.

Use axial coordinates for the triangular lattice, with basis vectors
\[
\mathbf e_1=(1,0),\qquad \mathbf e_2=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right).
\]
The hexagon of side length \(4\) is
\[
\{(a,b)\in \mathbb Z^2: |a|\le 4,\ |b|\le 4,\ |a+b|\le 4\}.
\]
It has \(61\) lattice vertices, one of which is the center \(O\). The other \(60\) vertices lie on rays from \(O\).

In one \(60^\circ\) sector, the primitive directions in increasing angular order are
\[
(1,0),\ (3,1),\ (2,1),\ (1,1),\ (1,2),\ (1,3).
\]
The numbers of lattice points on these rays, respectively, are
\[
4,\ 1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 1,\ 1.
\]
By rotating this sector \(60^\circ\) at a time, the \(36\) rays in counterclockwise order have multiplicities
\[
f=(4,1,1,2,1,1)
\]
repeated \(6\) times. Number the rays \(0,1,\dots,35\) in counterclockwise order, and let
\[
w_i=f(i\bmod 6).
\]

A triangle containing \(O\) strictly in its interior must use three distinct rays. For three distinct rays, \(O\) is strictly inside the triangle iff the three direction angles are not contained in any closed semicircle, equivalently iff all three angular gaps are strictly less than \(180^\circ\).

Since ray \(i+18\) is exactly opposite ray \(i\), an angular gap is \(<180^\circ\) exactly when the corresponding forward index gap is \(\le 17\). Thus a valid triangle corresponds to three ray indices whose positive cyclic gaps
\[
x,y,z,\qquad x+y+z=36
\]
all satisfy
\[
x,y,z\le 17.
\]

For a valid gap triple and a chosen starting ray \(i\), the number of triangles from those three rays is
\[
w_i w_{i+x} w_{i+x+y}.
\]
Each unordered triangle is counted \(3\) times this way, once for each starting ray.

Now group the gaps by residues modulo \(6\). Let
\[
N_{r,s}=\#\{(x,y): x,y,z\ge1,\ x+y+z=36,\ x,y,z\le17,\ x\equiv r,\ y\equiv s \pmod 6\}.
\]
Counting the allowed values of \(x\) and then the allowed residues of \(y\) gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|cccccc}
r & \text{allowed }x & s=0&1&2&3&4&5\\ \hline
0&6,12&1&3&3&3&3&3\\
1&7,13&3&3&3&3&3&3\\
2&2,8,14&3&3&3&3&3&6\\
3&3,9,15&3&3&3&3&6&6\\
4&4,10,16&3&3&3&6&6&6\\
5&5,11,17&3&3&6&6&6&6
\end{array}
\]

Also define
\[
A_{r,s}=\sum_{p=0}^5 f_p f_{p+r} f_{p+r+s},
\]
where all subscripts are modulo \(6\). Using
\[
f=(4,1,1,2,1,1),
\]
we compute

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
r\backslash s&0&1&2&3&4&5\\ \hline
0&76&28&28&52&28&28\\
1&28&18&24&24&18&28\\
2&28&24&18&24&28&18\\
3&52&24&24&52&24&24\\
4&28&18&28&24&18&24\\
5&28&28&18&24&24&18
\end{array}
\]

For each residue pair \((r,s)\), summing over the \(36\) starting rays contributes \(6A_{r,s}\) for each valid \((x,y)\). Since each triangle was counted \(3\) times, the desired number is
\[
2\sum_{r,s=0}^5 N_{r,s}A_{r,s}.
\]

Multiplying the two tables row by row gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
r & \sum_s N_{r,s}A_{r,s}\\ \hline
0&568\\
1&420\\
2&474\\
3&744\\
4&618\\
5&672
\end{array}
\]
so
\[
\sum_{r,s} N_{r,s}A_{r,s}
=568+420+474+744+618+672
=3496.
\]
Therefore the number of triangles is
\[
2\cdot 3496=6992.
\]

\[
\boxed{6992}
\]
